## Author’s thesis (paraphrased from source)

*MCDP 1* presents an institutional philosophy of warfighting rather than a catalogue of procedures. The Foreword describes it as the authoritative basis for how Marines fight and prepare to fight, offering broad concepts and values whose application necessarily requires judgment. It is meant to furnish a way of thinking that applies in war, crisis, and peace, and its intended audience includes all Marines rather than only commissioned officers. [AR] (Foreword)

The philosophy begins from an account of war as an interactive clash between independent human wills. War is violent, uncertain, fluid, disorderly, complex, and subject to friction and chance. Its conduct cannot be reduced to material quantities, scientific calculation, technology, or centrally controlled plans because moral and mental forces, local decisions, reciprocal adaptation, and human will exert decisive influence. [AR] (Ch 1, “War Defined”–“The Science, Art, and Dynamic of War,” pp. 3–19)

> “War is intrinsically unpredictable.”

[V] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” p. 7)

From that account, the publication derives a theory in which military action must serve policy, occurs simultaneously at strategic, operational, and tactical levels, and is shaped by the contest between initiative and response. Combat power is generated not only by destructive capacity but by the situational combination of physical, moral, and mental factors. Speed, focus, surprise, boldness, and the exploitation of critical vulnerabilities make it possible to produce effects disproportionate to numerical strength. [AR] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy”–“Creating and Exploiting Opportunity,” pp. 23–48)

> “The single most important thought to understand
> about our theory is that war must serve policy.”

[V] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” p. 23)

Preparation must embody the same philosophy expected in combat. Organisation, doctrine, training, education, personnel management, and equipment acquisition are all directed toward combat readiness. Because maneuver warfare relies on judgment, initiative, adaptation, and implicit cooperation, the institution must develop competent and trusted leaders at every level, tolerate honest mistakes arising from bold action, train under opposed and uncertain conditions, and resist technologies or administrative practices that centralise control. [AR] (Ch 3, “Force Planning”–“Equipping,” pp. 53–67)

The resulting doctrine is maneuver warfare: rapid, flexible, focused, and opportunistic action intended to shatter the enemy’s cohesion rather than merely reduce every physical component through cumulative attrition. Maneuver may create spatial, temporal, psychological, or technological advantage. Its command system is decentralised but unified through mission tactics, commander’s intent, a designated main effort, mutual trust, and a shared professional philosophy. [AR] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare”–“Main Effort,” pp. 72–92)

> “Maneuver warfare is a way of thinking in and about war
> that should shape our every action.”

[V] (Ch 4, “Conclusion,” p. 95)

## Part I: The nature of war

### War as an interactive clash of wills

War is defined as a violent clash of interests among organised groups characterised by military force. Although those groups have traditionally been states, the definition includes coalitions and factions inside or outside existing states when they possess political interests and can generate organised violence with significant political consequences. [AP] (Ch 1, “War Defined,” p. 3)

Its essence is not unilateral action against an inert target but reciprocal struggle between hostile, independent, and irreconcilable wills. Each belligerent acts, resists, adapts, and attempts to impose its will on the other. The publication uses Clausewitz’s image of wrestlers locked together to establish war as continuous mutual adaptation rather than execution against a passive object. [AR] (Ch 1, “War Defined,” pp. 3–4); [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” pp. 97–98)

Military violence or its credible threat is the means by which a belligerent seeks to impose its will. Violence may be directed narrowly against combatant forces or more broadly against a population, and hostilities may range from intense clashes between large forces to unconventional action barely reaching the threshold of violence. [AP] (Ch 1, “War Defined,” p. 4)

Perfect peace and total war are treated as theoretical extremes. Political groups normally coexist within a range containing economic competition, political and ideological tension, crises, civil disturbances, relief operations, unconventional hostilities, and potentially attempts to overturn an existing social or international order. Military force can enter that range at different points depending on the belligerents’ aims and cultures. [AP] (Ch 1, “War Defined,” pp. 4–5)

### Friction

Friction is the aggregate resistance that makes apparently simple actions difficult, consumes energy, and can make difficult actions seem impossible. It arises intrinsically from the interaction of opposed wills rather than being an occasional defect added to an otherwise orderly activity. [AP] (Ch 1, “Friction,” pp. 5–6)

The publication distinguishes mental friction, such as indecision, from physical friction, such as enemy fire or terrain. It also distinguishes external sources—enemy action, terrain, weather, and chance—from self-induced sources such as unclear goals, poor coordination, complicated plans, intricate command relationships, and burdensome technologies. Because war is human, every form of friction has psychological as well as physical effects. [AP] (Ch 1, “Friction,” pp. 5–6)

The practical requirement is not to imagine friction can be eliminated. Self-induced friction should be reduced, but forces must primarily develop the will to act effectively despite it while increasing the enemy’s friction until his capacity to fight weakens. Experience is indispensable because training can approximate but never fully reproduce combat’s friction. [AR] (Ch 1, “Friction,” p. 6)

Clausewitz supplies the governing formulation of friction as the force making the apparently easy difficult. The Notes identify *On War* as an essential treatment of war’s nature and theory for Marine officers. [BT] (Ch 1, “Friction,” p. 5; Notes, “The Nature of War,” pp. 97–98)

### Uncertainty, nonlinearity, risk, and chance

Uncertainty is pervasive enough to warrant treatment apart from friction. Information concerning the enemy, the environment, and friendly forces will remain incomplete, inaccurate, or contradictory despite collection efforts. Certainty is therefore not a realistic precondition for action. Judgment must work with possibilities and probabilities while recognising that apparently improbable events may have the greatest effects. [AR] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” pp. 7–8)

Nonlinearity means causes and effects can be disproportionate. Minor incidents and individual actions may determine battles, making prediction from inputs unreliable. The source supports this point through Clausewitz’s observation that outcomes may turn on incidents so small that history records them merely as anecdotes. [AP] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” p. 8); [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” pp. 97–98)

Uncertainty makes risk unavoidable in action and inaction alike. Greater prospective gain may demand greater risk, and concentrating combat power at a main effort requires accepting prudent risk elsewhere. The publication nevertheless distinguishes prudent risk from staking the whole prospect of success on one improbable occurrence. [AP] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” p. 8)

Chance consists of events neither side can reasonably foresee or control. It creates psychological friction but favours neither belligerent exclusively. The appropriate posture is therefore dual: treat chance as a threat while remaining ready to exploit the opportunities it creates. [AR] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” pp. 8–9)

The recommended responses to uncertainty are simple and flexible plans, preparation for likely contingencies, standing operating procedures, and initiative among subordinates. These measures enable effective action under uncertainty rather than purporting to remove it. [AP] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” p. 8)

### Fluidity and competitive rhythms

Every episode in war arises from a unique combination of circumstances, yet no episode stands alone. Each is shaped by preceding events and alters the conditions for what follows, producing a fluctuating continuum filled with unforeseen events and fleeting opportunities. Flexibility consists both in proactively shaping change and reacting rapidly when conditions shift. [AR] (Ch 1, “Fluidity,” p. 9)

Tempo fluctuates because people and equipment cannot sustain maximum activity indefinitely. Intense combat alternates with information gathering, replenishment, and redeployment. Darkness and weather influence the rhythm without necessarily stopping it, while each side tries to accelerate or exploit the rhythm to its own advantage. [AP] (Ch 1, “Fluidity,” pp. 9–10)

A second competitive rhythm operates between concentration and dispersion. Forces mass to concentrate combat power, but massing increases vulnerability to enemy fires and creates a need to disperse again. Each belligerent therefore attempts to concentrate temporarily while limiting exposure to the opponent’s concentration. [AP] (Ch 1, “Fluidity,” p. 10)

### Disorder

Friction, uncertainty, and fluidity drive war toward disorder. Plans fail, instructions are misunderstood, communications break down, and mistakes and unforeseen events accumulate. This disorder is simultaneously an impediment and a condition an opportunistic will can exploit. [AR] (Ch 1, “Disorder,” pp. 10–11)

> “The occurrences of war will not unfold like clockwork.”

[V] (Ch 1, “Disorder,” p. 11)

Encounters tend to become less like their original schemes as successive changes compel improvisation. Modern range, lethality, and dispersion further strain positive control, creating gaps, exposed flanks, unoccupied areas, and blurred distinctions between front and rear or friendly- and enemy-controlled areas. [AP] (Ch 1, “Disorder,” p. 11)

Precise control of every event is unattainable. Command can establish a broad framework and influence the flow of action, but it cannot make combat unfold mechanically. Success requires operating effectively amid disorder and, when possible, creating disorder in the enemy system and using it as a weapon. [AR] (Ch 1, “Disorder,” pp. 11–12)

### Complexity and distributed action

Each belligerent is a complex system rather than a single homogeneous intelligence. Divisions contain regiments, regiments contain battalions, and the hierarchy continues to fire teams and individual Marines. Every component belongs to a larger whole while possessing its own mission, local situation, decisions, and capacity to create friction for friend and enemy. [AP] (Ch 1, “Complexity,” p. 12)

Military action emerges from many interrelated local decisions taken simultaneously under incomplete information. This distributed character makes total centralisation and complete control by one decisionmaker inconsistent with war’s nature. [AR] (Ch 1, “Complexity,” pp. 12–13)

### The human dimension

The human dimension is central because war is a struggle of wills. Human nature introduces moral factors, emotions, inconsistencies, and behavioural differences into every conflict. Danger, fear, exhaustion, and privation affect combatants differently; an action that breaks one enemy’s will may harden another’s. Leadership-instilled will is presented as the driving force of action. [AP] (Ch 1, “The Human Dimension,” pp. 13–14)

Technological development and scientific calculation cannot make the human dimension disappear. A doctrine that reduces war to equipment, weapons, and force ratios neglects human will and is therefore judged inherently flawed. [AR] (Ch 1, “The Human Dimension,” p. 14)

The Notes recommend Guy Sajer’s *The Forgotten Soldier* as a first-hand account of human experience on the Eastern Front and S. L. A. Marshall’s *Men Against Fire* as an insightful, though methodologically criticised, study of human reactions to combat. [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” p. 98)

### Violence, danger, fear, and courage

> “War is among the greatest horrors known to humanity; it
> should never be romanticized.”

[V] (Ch 1, “Violence and Danger,” p. 14)

Violence or its credible threat is the essential means of war, with bloodshed, destruction, and suffering as immediate results. Although its magnitude varies with aims and means, the publication rejects any treatment that obscures war’s violent essence. [AR] (Ch 1, “Violence and Danger,” p. 14)

The Notes reinforce this claim through Clausewitz’s rejection of the idea that war can be made harmless through kindness. They present denial of war’s brutality as both futile and dangerous because mistakes arising from a sentimental refusal to confront violence can be especially damaging. [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” p. 98)

Fear is a universal response to danger and corrodes will. Courage is not freedom from fear but the strength to overcome it. Because fear and courage vary across people and situations, leaders must understand them rather than assume uniform reactions. [AP] (Ch 1, “Violence and Danger,” pp. 14–15)

Realistic training and experience under fire can lessen combat’s mystique and increase confidence. Trusted leadership, unit cohesion, esprit, and individual self-confidence help people act despite fear; concern for the respect and trust of comrades may outweigh personal fear. [AP] (Ch 1, “Violence and Danger,” p. 15)

### Physical, moral, and mental forces

Physical forces include measurable matters such as weapon capabilities, supplies, force ratios, casualties, terrain, prisoners, and captured materiel. Moral forces encompass psychological and ethical factors such as national resolve, conscience, emotion, fear, courage, morale, leadership, and esprit. Mental forces provide the intellectual capacity to understand complex situations, estimate, decide, devise strategies and tactics, and plan. [AP] (Ch 1, “Physical, Moral, and Mental Forces,” pp. 15–16)

Although physical factors are more readily quantified, moral and mental forces are said to exert greater influence over war’s nature and outcome. Physical action often achieves its greatest effect through its impact on moral strength: fires, for example, matter not only through destruction but through what that destruction does to enemy will. [AR] (Ch 1, “Physical, Moral, and Mental Forces,” pp. 16–17)

Napoleon’s reported maxim that the moral relates to the material as three to one is cited as a borrowed numerical expression of this priority, not as a calculation developed by the publication itself. [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” p. 98)

### War’s continuity and evolution

War is treated as timeless in basic nature but continuously changing in means and methods. Technological and organisational developments can gradually alter warfare or abruptly disrupt its equilibrium, as occurred with the rifled bore, mass conscription, and the railroad. [AP] (Ch 1, “The Evolution of War,” p. 17)

Technology changes capabilities, but tactics, operations, and strategy must adapt both to exploit friendly developments and counter enemy ones. The belligerent that first exploits an important development gains a significant advantage, while ignorance of change leaves a force unequal to new challenges. [AR] (Ch 1, “The Evolution of War,” pp. 17–18)

The Foreword applies this principle to doctrine itself. It argues that an adaptive doctrine cannot stagnate and explains the 1997 revision as an effort to improve the account of complexity and unpredictability, broaden the treatment of modern conflict, and clarify styles of warfare, commander’s intent, main effort, and critical vulnerability without abandoning the earlier publication’s central message. [AR] (Foreword)

### Science, art, and competitive human dynamics

The science of war concerns matters governed methodically by empirical laws, including ballistics, mechanics, fires, weapon effects, movement, and resupply. Science is necessary but does not describe the whole phenomenon. [AP] (Ch 1, “The Science, Art, and Dynamic of War,” pp. 17–18)

The art of war is the creative and situational employment of knowledge through judgment, intuition, and experience. It subsumes science by applying it to unique conditions and includes devising strategies, tactics, and practical plans. Art, however, also stops short of explaining war’s complete dynamic. [AP] (Ch 1, “The Science, Art, and Dynamic of War,” p. 18)

The fundamental dynamic is competitive human interaction. People in conflict do not behave like chemicals in a formula or materials in an artwork; their interaction calls for fortitude, perseverance, boldness, esprit, and will. The publication therefore concludes that war requires scientific knowledge and artistic creativity but is ultimately driven by human competition and will. [AR] (Ch 1, “The Science, Art, and Dynamic of War,” pp. 18–20)

## Part II: The theory of war

### War as policy and politics

Politics concerns the dynamic distribution of power through cooperation and competition, while policy consists of consciously established objectives produced within that process. The concepts are related but not interchangeable. Policy aims must determine the conduct of war, and military action remains subordinate to them. [AP] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” p. 23)

The scale and form of violence should vary with the political object. Unlimited aims may align with war’s destructive tendency, while limited aims are more likely to require political restrictions on force. Such restrictions can be correct, but military leaders must warn political authorities when constraints jeopardise the assigned military mission. [AR] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” pp. 23–24)

Policy must also be reconciled with available means. Objectives beyond military capability should not be adopted, and many political problems cannot be solved by military force. Even where military action can contribute, war is an animate and interactive force whose course and unintended consequences can change the political situation itself. [AR] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” pp. 23–24)

War is not exclusively political: social, cultural, and psychological factors also shape its conduct and its usefulness for solving political problems. Clausewitz is used to support the narrower proposition that war continues political intercourse through the addition of other means rather than replacing politics with an isolated military sphere. [AP] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” p. 24); [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 99–100)

### Incapacitation and erosion

The first broad way to impose will is to render the enemy helpless by destroying or disabling his military capacity. The source calls this a strategy of annihilation but prefers incapacitation when necessary to avoid implying that every enemy person and item of equipment must be physically destroyed. This strategy suits an unlimited political objective or a situation in which resistance is expected to continue as long as any military means remain. [AP] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” pp. 24–25)

The second way is a strategy of erosion: use force to make continued resistance more painful than accepting the imposed terms. Rather than eliminating every means of resistance, it raises costs beyond what enemy leadership is prepared to bear and is associated with limited political goals the enemy might ultimately accept. [AP] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” p. 25)

The Notes attribute the annihilation–erosion distinction to Hans Delbrück’s history of war. They explain that classical theory commonly calls the second strategy attrition, while *MCDP 1* uses erosion to prevent confusion with tactical attrition warfare. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 100)

### Means and the spectrum of conflict

War can draw on economic, diplomatic, military, and psychological power. The publication focuses on military force but insists it not be considered independently from other elements of national power. Military use can range from deployment as a demonstration of resolve and enforcement of a negotiated truce to general warfare. [AP] (Ch 2, “Means in War,” pp. 25–26)

Conflict forms a spectrum defined partly by the magnitude of violence. At one end, military operations other than war employ military capabilities selectively to deter war, resolve conflict, promote peace, or support civil authorities. At the other, general war involves sustained, large-scale combat. Policy objectives, means, national will, and the density of combat power help determine a conflict’s position on the spectrum. [AP] (Ch 2, “The Spectrum of Conflict,” pp. 26–27)

Intensity is not uniform within a conflict and can escalate or decline over time. High-intensity episodes may occur inside operations other than war, while major conflicts may contain quiet phases or sectors. Belligerents may escalate when existing means fail or de-escalate when they cannot sustain the initial intensity. [AP] (Ch 2, “The Spectrum of Conflict,” pp. 26–27)

Military operations other than war and small wars are described as more probable than major regional or general war, but they are not merely scaled-down versions of general war. A force optimised for technologically sophisticated conventional warfare may be poorly prepared for conflict against a lightly equipped guerrilla opponent. The Marine Corps therefore requires versatility across the whole spectrum. [AR] (Ch 2, “The Spectrum of Conflict,” pp. 27–28)

### Strategic, operational, and tactical levels

The strategic level focuses directly on policy objectives and applies in peace as well as war. National strategy coordinates all elements of national power, while military strategy applies military force within that larger design. Strategy establishes goals, assigns forces and assets, and sets conditions governing force; political objectives remain the authoritative basis for operations. [AP] (Ch 2, “Levels of War,” p. 28)

The tactical level concerns concepts and methods for accomplishing particular missions. In combat, it applies combat power to defeat an enemy at a particular time and place; outside combat, it includes methods for missions such as maintaining order and security. Tactics requires judgment and creativity and is distinguished from repetitive techniques and procedures, although the two overlap. [AP] (Ch 2, “Levels of War,” pp. 28–30)

The operational level links tactical results to strategic objectives. It determines when, where, and under what conditions to accept or refuse battle, works across broader spans of time and space than tactics, and uses engagements and battles as the means for winning campaigns. [AP] (Ch 2, “Levels of War,” p. 30)

The levels are conceptual distinctions rather than sealed domains. In large conventional wars they may be relatively distinct; in nuclear war or military operations other than war they may compress until one commander acts at two or three levels. A small-unit action can then carry direct strategic consequences. [AP] (Ch 2, “Levels of War,” pp. 31–32)

The Notes borrow formal definitions of all three levels, national strategy, and military strategy from *Joint Publication 1-02*. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 100–102)

### Initiative and response

Every action either takes the initiative or responds to the opponent. Initiative dictates the conflict’s terms, pursues a positive aim, and is the preferred form because it is the means for imposing one’s will. Response usually has the negative object of blocking or counteracting enemy intentions, although a response may seek to seize the initiative in turn. [AR] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” pp. 32–33)

War’s flux emerges from continuous interaction between these modes. Both sides may initially seek the initiative, but one gains an advantage and compels the other to respond until the disadvantaged party can reverse the relationship. [AP] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” p. 33)

### Offense, defense, and the culminating point

Offense contributes striking power and is commonly associated with initiative. Defense contributes resisting and preserving power and is commonly associated with response. These associations are not absolute: a defense can hold the initiative by compelling attack against strength or by drawing an enemy into an ambush. [AP] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” pp. 33–34)

Defense tends to expend less energy, but this does not make it inherently stronger. Its advantages depend on the situation, and effective defense cannot be purely passive. Its decisive expression is the counterattack—Clausewitz’s shield composed of well-directed blows—so offense exists inside defense. [AR] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” p. 34); [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 102)

Defense likewise exists inside offense. An attacking force must halt, replenish, and defend at some times and places; concentrating for offense also requires accepting defensive postures elsewhere. [AP] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” p. 34)

An offensive usually weakens as it advances through casualties and expenditure of fuel, ammunition, physical strength, and sometimes morale. It eventually reaches a culminating point beyond which attack cannot be sustained. At that moment, the attack’s defensive component is especially vulnerable to an enemy counterattack. [AR] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” pp. 34–35)

Offense and defense consequently coexist and transition fluidly. They can also nest across levels: a tactical defense may support an offensive campaign, or a local counterattack may seize initiative within a larger response. [AP] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” p. 35)

### Attrition warfare

Attrition warfare seeks victory through cumulative material destruction by superior firepower. It treats war principally as a direct contest of strength and force ratios, regards the enemy as a collection of targets, and searches for enemy concentrations as efficient targets. Progress is measured quantitatively through destruction, casualties, and terrain. [AP] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” pp. 36–37)

Maneuver has a subordinate role in this style, positioning fires more efficiently rather than attacking the enemy system. The focus on volume, accuracy, procedure, and efficiency tends toward centralised control and requires the capacity both to inflict and absorb attrition. Material and numerical superiority become the principal prerequisites, making war an industrial as well as a military problem. [AR] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” pp. 36–37)

The publication offers the Western Front in the First World War, French defensive operations in May 1940, the Allied campaign in Italy in 1943–1944, Eisenhower’s broad-front offensive after Normandy, later operations in Korea, and most United States operations in Vietnam as examples with high attritional content. [AE] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” p. 37)

### Maneuver warfare as a contrasting style

Maneuver warfare seeks to circumvent a problem and attack from advantage rather than meet strength directly. Its object is systemic incapacitation: components may remain physically intact but lose the ability to operate as a cohesive whole. Enemy concentrations are treated as strengths to avoid, while friendly strength is focused against selected weakness. [AR] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” pp. 37–38)

Success depends on understanding the specific enemy system, identifying vulnerabilities, and using speed and surprise to concentrate strength against weakness. Tempo becomes a weapon. Effects may be disproportionate to effort, although inept maneuver carries a corresponding possibility of catastrophic failure. [AP] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” p. 38)

Firepower and attrition remain essential inside maneuver warfare. At a critical point, selected enemy elements may be annihilated, but their destruction serves the larger purpose of disabling the enemy system rather than contributing merely to an incremental total. [AR] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” p. 38)

Examples with substantial maneuver content include Allenby’s 1918 Palestine campaign, German operations in 1939–1941 and especially the 1940 invasion of France, the unsuccessful Allied attempt at Anzio, Patton’s breakout from Normandy, MacArthur’s Inchon campaign, and III Marine Amphibious Force’s combined action programme in Vietnam. The Anzio example is included despite failure because the attempted design sought to bypass attritional fighting; the Vietnam example attacked the Viet Cong system through its popular support base. [AE] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” pp. 38–39)

Pure attrition and pure maneuver do not occur in practice. All warfare combines them, and the prevailing balance depends on friendly capabilities and the enemy’s nature. The Marine Corps locates its doctrine principally toward maneuver. [AP] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” p. 39)

The Notes identify Edward Luttwak’s *Strategy: The Logic of War and Peace* as a source for the attrition–maneuver spectrum and further historical examples. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 102)

### Combat power

Combat power is the total destructive force available against the enemy at a given time. Its components range from measurable numbers to less tangible effects of geography, maneuver, tempo, surprise, offense and defense, direction of attack, morale, perseverance, and leadership. [AP] (Ch 2, “Combat Power,” pp. 39–40)

The publication refuses to list, index, or assign fixed values to all components because every combination is temporary and situationally unique. A fixed formula would contradict the account of war developed in Chapter 1. [AR] (Ch 2, “Combat Power,” p. 40)

The formal definition of combat power is borrowed from *Joint Publication 1-02*, while Clausewitz is cited for numerical superiority as the most common element in victory. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 102)

### Speed and focus

Speed encompasses rapidity over time and space. Speed over time is tempo; speed over space is rapid movement. Relative speed matters more than absolute speed because superiority allows a force to seize initiative, dictate terms, improve security, enable surprise and maneuver, and concentrate strength at the decisive place. [AP] (Ch 2, “Speed and Focus,” pp. 40–41)

High speed cannot be maintained indefinitely, so combat develops another competitive rhythm of acceleration, slowing, and renewed acceleration. Each belligerent tries to generate speed when it confers advantage and to degrade the opponent’s speed. [AP] (Ch 2, “Speed and Focus,” p. 41)

Focus is the convergence of effects at a particular time and place. It can give a numerically inferior force decisive local superiority, but it demands economy and acceptance of risk elsewhere. Spending resources on unnecessary efforts or over-resourcing secondary ones violates focus. [AP] (Ch 2, “Speed and Focus,” p. 41)

Focus applies temporally as well as spatially and extends from combat to preparation. It is achieved through cooperation among all elements, including ground combat, aviation, and combat service support. Combined speed and focus create the shock effect sought in action. [AP] (Ch 2, “Speed and Focus,” pp. 41–42)

The Notes link tempo to John Boyd’s observation–orientation–decision–action cycle. A belligerent that repeatedly completes the cycle faster gains a cumulative advantage as enemy reactions become progressively later and less effective. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 102–103)

### Surprise

Surprise is enemy disorientation produced by an unexpected event. It does not require complete unawareness; it is enough that awareness arrives too late for effective reaction. Surprise is both a condition for local superiority and an independent source of combat power because its psychological effects can exceed the physical means employed. [AP] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” pp. 42–43)

Surprise depends on the severity of disorientation and the enemy’s capacity to recover. At its extreme it creates temporary shock and inability to react. Its advantages are fleeting, friction works against it, and success depends partly on enemy expectations and preparedness rather than solely on friendly action. It is therefore decisive when achieved but dangerous as the only margin for victory. [AR] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” p. 43)

Three methods are distinguished. Deception gives the enemy a clear but false picture and induces harmful action. Ambiguity prevents the enemy from knowing which possibility to prepare for. Stealth denies knowledge of impending action altogether. Deception promises the greatest effect but is the hardest to achieve. [AP] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” pp. 43–44)

### Boldness

Boldness exploits uncertainty without hesitation in pursuit of major rather than marginal results. It can take the form of immediate aggressive action or patient calculation that allows the enemy to become irreversibly committed before striking. [AP] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” p. 44)

Boldness must arise from situational awareness and judgment; otherwise it becomes recklessness. Once the situation has been weighed, half measures squander surprise. Risk acceptance can make surprise possible, while surprise magnifies the effects of bold action. [AR] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” pp. 44–45)

Clausewitz is cited for treating boldness as a genuinely creative force with power beyond calculations of time, space, and force. [BT] (Ch 2, “Surprise and Boldness,” p. 44; Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 103)

### Centers of gravity and critical vulnerabilities

A belligerent is a system of unequal physical, moral, and mental components and relationships. Centers of gravity are important sources of strength whose loss would seriously reduce the enemy’s capacity or will. They may be intangible qualities, military capabilities, locations, or relationships among organisations and forces. Friendly centers should be protected; enemy centers should be removed. [AP] (Ch 2, “Centers of Gravity and Critical Vulnerabilities,” pp. 45–46)

A critical vulnerability is a weakness whose exploitation would cause especially significant damage to the enemy’s ability to resist. The object is not merely to locate any weak point but to identify one connected to a consequential enemy strength. [AP] (Ch 2, “Centers of Gravity and Critical Vulnerabilities,” pp. 46–47)

The concepts are complementary perspectives on the same targeting problem. A center of gravity asks which source of enemy strength matters most; a critical vulnerability asks which weakness offers a pathway to affecting such strength. Both focus combat power for maximum effect. [AR] (Ch 2, “Centers of Gravity and Critical Vulnerabilities,” p. 47)

Enemy systems may lack a single decisive center, or that center may be well protected. Several lesser centers or vulnerabilities may therefore need to be attacked simultaneously or in sequence. The publication cautions against multiplying them unnecessarily because a relatively small set better supports focus. [AP] (Ch 2, “Centers of Gravity and Critical Vulnerabilities,” p. 47)

Clausewitz supplies part of the conceptual lineage, and the Notes reproduce the *Joint Publication 1-02* definition of centers of gravity as characteristics, capabilities, or localities from which a military force derives freedom of action, strength, or will. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 103)

### Creating and exploiting opportunity

When critical vulnerabilities cannot be confidently identified in advance, commanders may have to exploit successive vulnerabilities until action reveals a decisive opportunity. Opportunities emerge from friendly actions, enemy mistakes, friction, fog, and chance. Exploiting one opportunity can generate others. [AR] (Ch 2, “Creating and Exploiting Opportunity,” p. 48)

Decisive exploitation requires speed, flexibility, boldness, and initiative. The publication gives special weight to the willingness to exploit opportunities ruthlessly rather than waiting for a fully predetermined opening. [AP] (Ch 2, “Creating and Exploiting Opportunity,” p. 48)

## Part III: Preparing for war

### Readiness and force planning

In peace, the military’s principal task is preparation for war. Readiness contributes to deterrence, and the Marine Corps’ expeditionary role requires preparedness for immediate employment across environments and types of conflict. Training, organisation, equipment, leadership, and doctrine must therefore converge on combat readiness. [AR] (Ch 3, introduction, p. 53)

Force planning creates and maintains military capabilities. It begins with a clearly defined readiness objective and is concept-based: operating concepts describe likely missions and how forces may perform them, which in turn identify required capabilities and coordinate programmes to develop them. [AP] (Ch 3, “Force Planning,” pp. 53–54)

The process integrates training, education, doctrine, organisation, personnel management, and acquisition. Unity of effort is required in preparation just as in combat. [AP] (Ch 3, “Force Planning,” p. 54)

The formal force-planning definition is borrowed from *Joint Publication 1-02*. [BT] (Notes, “Preparing for War,” pp. 103–104)

### Organisation and the MAGTF

Operating forces must be forward-deployed or rapidly deployable and capable of expeditionary operations. Amphibious capability remains distinctive, but forces must also deploy by whatever means a situation requires. Active forces should respond immediately to most crises, with the Reserve establishment augmenting sustained missions. [AP] (Ch 3, “Organization,” pp. 54–55)

Marine air-ground task forces combine ground, aviation, combat service support, and command elements under one commander. They have no standard structure; each is tailored to the situation and can be restructured as conditions change. [AP] (Ch 3, “Organization,” p. 55)

Organisation should be designed for war and adapted to peace rather than the reverse. Tables of organisation should prioritise deployability and task organisation, with type-based organisation retained only as training, administrative, and logistic requirements demand. Habitual supported–supporting relationships should build familiarity without preventing nonstandard arrangements when needed. [AR] (Ch 3, “Organization,” p. 55)

### Doctrine

Doctrine teaches the Marine Corps’ fundamental beliefs about war’s nature, theory, preparation, and conduct. It establishes a way of thinking and fighting, a philosophy of combat leadership, a professional mandate, and a common language that supports harmonious action and mutual understanding. [AP] (Ch 3, “Doctrine,” pp. 55–56)

Doctrine is authoritative but not prescriptive. It supplies general guidance requiring judgment rather than procedures intended for mechanical application to particular situations. [AR] (Ch 3, “Doctrine,” p. 56)

The Notes reproduce the corresponding *Joint Publication 1-02* definition, including the principle that doctrine is authoritative while requiring judgment in application. [BT] (Notes, “Preparing for War,” p. 104)

### Professional competence, action, and responsibility

Marine leaders must combine intellectual understanding of military art with the practical ability to act. They are expected to be resolute and self-reliant in decision and energetic in execution, while recognising that the resources spent in war include human lives. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” pp. 56–57)

> “The military profession is a thinking profession.”

[V] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 57)

Every Marine is expected to study the art and science of war. Officers in particular require foundations in military theory and history, not as decoration but as preparation for judgment and action. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 57)

The chapter epigraph from Hans von Seeckt treats action as a sequence of thought, preparation, and execution governed by will; character without intellect is dangerous, but intellect without will is worthless. [BT] (Ch 3 epigraph; Notes, “Preparing for War,” p. 103)

### Initiative, mistakes, and the rejection of zero defects

Maneuver warfare requires intelligent leaders inclined toward boldness and initiative at the lowest levels. Initiative is willingness to act on one’s judgment and is a prerequisite for boldness. Both can become rash when carried too far, but mistakes arising from junior leaders’ overboldness are treated as a necessary part of learning. [AR] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 57)

The publication rejects a zero-defects mentality because fear of punishment suppresses initiative. Lenience toward honest overboldness does not remove counselling, constructive criticism, discipline, or responsibility; nor does it permit stupidity or recklessness. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 57)

Errors of inaction and timidity warrant more severe treatment. Lack of orders is not accepted as justification when the situation demands initiative, and avoidance of responsibility or necessary risk is not tolerated. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” pp. 57–58)

Clausewitz is cited for distinguishing laudable, even ill-timed boldness from boldness that deliberately violates an expressed order. The former signals a rich organisational capacity for daring; the latter must be disciplined because obedience remains essential. [BT] (Notes, “Preparing for War,” p. 104)

### Trust, candour, and decision support

Trust must run in both directions: seniors trust subordinates’ abilities, and subordinates trust seniors’ competence and support. It must be earned through demonstrated professional skill, familiarity, shared experience, and common philosophy. Conduct that undermines it warrants strict censure. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 58)

Before a decision, subordinates have a duty to provide honest professional opinions even when they disagree with the senior. After the commander decides, juniors must support the decision as their own. Seniors must encourage candour rather than rely on rank to suppress disagreement, and compliant yes-men seeking advancement are explicitly rejected. [AR] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 58)

### Training for combat

Training exists to develop forces capable of winning in combat and is therefore the main effort of a peacetime military. It must continue during war so that forces adapt to combat lessons. [AP] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 59)

Entry-level training provides a shared experience, heritage, values, and bond of comradeship. Individual combat skills form an essential foundation for every Marine regardless of speciality, but unit skill is not merely the sum of individual proficiency. [AP] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 59)

Senior commanders must grant subordinate units enough time and freedom to train autonomously. Training, like combat, should be decentralised: seniors establish goals, standards, intent, and a main effort but ordinarily avoid dictating how subordinates achieve them. [AR] (Ch 3, “Training,” pp. 59–60)

Training should progress from individual and small-unit skills to a fully combined-arms MAGTF. As far as possible, units should train in their combat organisation with the assigned, reinforcing, and supporting forces they will require. [AP] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 60)

Drills use repetition to build speed and coordination in standardised tasks that should not vary, such as gun drills, preflight preparation, and immediate actions. Exercises instead develop tactical judgment under simulated combat conditions. [AP] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 60)

Only opposed, free-play exercises can adequately practise the art of war because they introduce an independent will together with uncertainty, stress, disorder, and friction. Canned scenarios remove the reciprocal opposition that the publication identifies as war’s essence. [AR] (Ch 3, “Training,” pp. 60–61)

### Critiques

Critiques support improvement through prompt, critical self-analysis even after success. They should occur before memories fade and should invite open contributions from all participants. [AP] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 61)

Mistakes and successes are both learning material, so participants must be willing to acknowledge errors and commanders must tolerate that candour. Since situations are unique, critiques should focus less on mechanically approving or condemning actions and more on why those actions were chosen and why they produced their results. [AR] (Ch 3, “Training,” p. 61)

### Professional military education

Professional military education is a continuous, progressive process for developing creative and thoughtful leaders. Early career development resembles an apprenticeship: leaders acquire theoretical foundations while learning the techniques and procedures of a particular field and seek mastery at the tactical level. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” pp. 61–62)

As officers progress, their mastery should expand to the operational level, combined arms, amphibious warfare, and expeditionary operations. Senior officers should be able to articulate and integrate MAGTF capabilities in joint and multinational settings and understand the art of war across all levels. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” p. 62)

Responsibility is three-tiered. Formal schools contribute structured education; commanders develop subordinates through teaching and unit programmes; and individuals undertake self-directed professional study. No tier can substitute completely for the others. [AR] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” pp. 62–64)

Schools should develop military judgment rather than rely on rote instruction. Commanders should treat subordinate development as a principal command responsibility and use reading, map exercises, war games, battle studies, and terrain studies. The development of subordinates reflects directly on the commander. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” p. 63)

> “Finally, every Marine has an individual responsibility to
> study the profession of arms.”

[V] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” p. 63)

A leader without interest in military history and theory possesses the appearance rather than the substance of leadership. Intellectual study is placed alongside physical conditioning, especially for officers, whose minds are described as their principal weapons. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” pp. 63–64)

### Personnel management

Because war is human and maneuver warfare depends on individual judgment, Marines of the same grade and speciality cannot be treated as interchangeable. Assignments should reflect ability and temperament, including differing suitability for command and staff roles without penalising either. [AP] (Ch 3, “Personnel Management,” p. 64)

Personnel stability builds cohesion, teamwork, and implicit understanding. Although combat casualties inevitably disrupt stability, a cohesive unit is better prepared to absorb losses and integrate replacements. Promotion should reward responsibility and initiative. [AP] (Ch 3, “Personnel Management,” pp. 64–65)

### Equipping for doctrine and expeditionary use

Equipment should be reliable, maintainable, easy to operate, interoperable, and consistent with doctrine and tactics. It should minimise specialised training and account for Marine dependence on shipping, landing craft, helicopters, and vertical or short take-off and landing aircraft, as well as operations in undeveloped theatres with limited infrastructure. [AP] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 65)

Existing off-the-shelf capabilities should be exploited to reduce development costs and fielding time. Acquisition is a two-way process: future requirements should follow operating concepts and, where possible, analysis of likely enemy vulnerabilities, while useful existing equipment should not be overlooked. [AP] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” pp. 65–66)

Equipment contributes only when its combat value justifies training, maintenance, fuel or power, transportation, and other support demands. Acquisition should balance specialised capability against broad utility and may preserve a variety of equipment types rather than depend on one increasingly specialised and counterable family. [AP] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 66)

Employment techniques, procedures, and operator training should be developed before or alongside fielding so that new equipment becomes operationally useful without avoidable delay. [AP] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 66)

### Technology’s two dangers

One danger is overreliance. Technology can improve the means of war but cannot remove human beings from warfare, cure every deficiency, or provide permanent advantage. Countermeasures will reduce any technological edge, and forces must remain capable when equipment fails. [AR] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 67)

The opposite danger is failing to use technological capability effectively. The publication does not reject technology; it requires disciplined use aligned with doctrine and tactics. Advanced information systems become harmful when they tempt commanders to impose the precise positive control that decentralised command rejects. [AR] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 67)

Preparation and conduct are inseparable. Military activity not contributing to a current war is justified only insofar as it prepares for a possible future one, because failure in preparation produces battlefield disaster. [AR] (Ch 3, “Conclusion,” pp. 67–68)

## Part IV: The conduct of war

### The doctrinal challenge

The Marine Corps’ stated justification is to secure or protect national policy objectives by military force when peaceful means alone cannot do so. Its conduct of war must follow from the preceding account of war’s nature and theory and must guide preparation. [AP] (Ch 4, introduction, p. 71)

The required concept must function across the spectrum of conflict and exploit uncertainty, disorder, fluidity, time competition, moral and mental forces, and fleeting opportunity. It must work without assuming numerical superiority and, especially in expeditionary situations, must permit rapid success against a larger enemy with limited casualties and external support. [AR] (Ch 4, “The Challenge,” pp. 71–72)

### Maneuver in multiple dimensions

Traditional maneuver seeks spatial advantage through movement. *MCDP 1* broadens the concept to any action generating an exploitable advantage, including psychological, technological, and temporal advantage. Maneuver in time means operating at a faster tempo so an inferior force can create decisive superiority at the necessary time and place. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 72)

Maneuver warfare seeks to shatter enemy cohesion through rapid, focused, and unexpected actions that create a turbulent situation deteriorating faster than the enemy can manage. It penetrates or bypasses defenses to disrupt the enemy system rather than wearing down every component in sequence. [AR] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” pp. 72–73)

The immediate object is an enemy unable to function as a coordinated whole. Physical components may remain, but once moral, mental, and physical cohesion is broken they lose their systemic value. Remaining individuals and small units can then be defeated more easily because their ability to fight collectively has been destroyed. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 73)

### Firepower within maneuver warfare

Firepower is central rather than opposed to maneuver. Enemy forces should be physically destroyed when that action supports the larger purpose, and selected enemy elements may suffer extreme attrition where friendly combat power is focused against critical weakness. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” pp. 73–74)

The distinction lies in purpose. Destruction is not accumulated mechanically until the entire enemy is worn away; it contributes to systemic disruption. Firepower’s greatest effect is often the disorganisation and moral shock it causes rather than the slow sum of physical damage. [AR] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 74)

### Dilemmas, tempo, and relentless exploitation

Maneuver warfare presents the enemy with menacing dilemmas and events occurring more quickly than he can understand and answer. Each late reaction increases his disorientation until events overtake his ability to resist. [AR] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 74)

Speed seizes initiative and keeps the enemy off balance; focus concentrates violence and shock against vulnerabilities. Once an advantage is found or created, it must be pressed without hesitation. At a decisive opportunity, the publication calls for committing all available combat power and accepting exhaustion to exploit the opening fully. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” pp. 74–75)

Surprise is cultivated by understanding and shaping enemy expectations through deception, avoiding fixed rules and recognisable patterns, and operating along axes that preserve several possible courses of action. Ambiguity keeps the enemy uncertain about which course will be chosen. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 75)

The human qualities demanded include endurance, courage, tolerance for uncertainty, mental flexibility, independence, initiative, boldness, opportunism, and moral courage in accepting responsibility. These must remain disciplined by loyalty to higher objectives and the ability to think above one’s level. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” pp. 75–76)

### Orienting on the enemy system

Maneuver warfare directs attention outward toward the particular enemy rather than inward toward flawless execution of predetermined procedures. The enemy system means the specific entity confronting a Marine at the relevant level. [AR] (Ch 4, “Orienting on the Enemy,” pp. 76–77)

For a pilot, the system may include radars, surface-to-air missiles, and aircraft obstructing access to a target. For a rifle company commander, it may consist of mutually supporting positions, obstacles, and crew-served weapons. For an electronic-warfare specialist, it may be command-and-control networks; for a Marine expeditionary force commander, it may include combat formations and their command, logistics, and intelligence organisations. [AE] (Ch 4, “Orienting on the Enemy,” p. 76)

The force should understand what makes that system function, then penetrate and disassemble it by striking critical vulnerabilities and centers of gravity. A fortified defense, for example, may be defeated by infiltration or a narrow attack at a weak point, followed by envelopment or lateral attack from inside, rather than by frontal destruction of each position. [AE] (Ch 4, “Orienting on the Enemy,” pp. 76–77)

Understanding must be on the enemy’s own terms. Commanders must not assume the enemy thinks, fights, values, or pursues objectives in the same way they do. [AP] (Ch 4, “Orienting on the Enemy,” p. 77)

### Decentralised command

Command and control must be decentralised to generate tempo and cope with disorder. Subordinates act on their understanding of senior intent rather than routinely forwarding information and waiting for decisions to return. A competent commander at the point of decision will often understand the local situation better than a distant senior. [AR] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” pp. 77–78)

The philosophy is based on human characteristics rather than equipment and procedure. Communications systems and staff processes may assist command, but they must not suppress personality, imagination, initiative, boldness, or strength of will. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 78)

### Implicit communication

Implicit communication uses shared understanding, concise familiar expressions, and anticipation of another’s thinking rather than exhaustive instructions. It is developed through mutual trust, a shared philosophy, and shared experience. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” pp. 78–79)

Practical consequences include stable working relationships, direct conversation between key leaders, oral communication when possible so tone and inflection carry meaning, and in-person communication when gestures and bearing matter. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 79)

The Notes attribute the command application of implicit communication to John Boyd’s “An Organic Design for Command and Control.” [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 105)

### Commanding forward

Commanders normally position themselves where they can best influence events, often well forward. Direct observation helps them sense combat’s rhythm, obtain understanding unavailable from reports, exert personal influence at decisive points, and avoid information delays and distortions. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 79)

Physical presence also demonstrates willingness to share danger and privation, supporting subordinate trust. Forward command must not become oversupervision, however, and it must be balanced against the need to retain awareness of the whole situation from a more central location. [AR] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” pp. 79–80)

### Thriving amid uncertainty and disorder

Maneuver warfare is particularly disorderly because it emphasises initiative and speed. Commanders who wait for certainty, seek continuous positive control, or attempt to force events into a precise plan deny war’s nature. The preferred posture is to cope with chaos and use it against an opponent who adapts less effectively. [AR] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 80)

In practical terms, forces should act without waiting for certainty, avoid excessive control that slows tempo, reject formulaic order, and abandon plans that have outlived their usefulness. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” pp. 80–81)

This command philosophy applies in peace as well as combat. Subordinates conditioned to oversupervision in garrison cannot be expected suddenly to display boldness and initiative in the field. Training, acquisition, administration, and routine duties should cultivate the same habits required in war. [AR] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 81)

A decentralised system requires competent leadership throughout the hierarchy, not merely one competent senior. It also depends on familiarity, implicit understanding, and reciprocal confidence between seniors and subordinates. [AP] (Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” p. 81)

### Shaping the action

Because victory is not conceived as the mere accumulation of enemy losses, commanders require a larger scheme explaining how they intend to win. They first identify what is to be accomplished, why it matters, and how action will connect critical vulnerabilities to enemy centers of gravity and mission accomplishment. [AR] (Ch 4, “Shaping the Action,” p. 82)

Commanders also view friendly forces through enemy eyes to identify their own vulnerabilities and anticipate hostile action. Ideally, actions before an engagement shape time and space so decisively that the eventual result follows from conditions already created. [AP] (Ch 4, “Shaping the Action,” p. 82)

Planning projects thought forward but should not impose a detailed timetable on an inherently disorderly future. Shaping uses lethal and nonlethal activity ranging from direct attack and electronic warfare to psychological operations and stockpiling supplies. [AP] (Ch 4, “Shaping the Action,” pp. 82–83)

Examples include canalising movement, delaying reinforcements to fight a divided enemy, deceiving the enemy to create exploitable expectations, and destroying air defenses so friendly aviation can operate effectively. Shaping should preserve several future options rather than locking the force into one course. [AE] (Ch 4, “Shaping the Action,” p. 83)

Influence decreases with distance into the future, so plans should become less precise the farther ahead they look. Senior commanders shape theatres over weeks or months; junior commanders shape immediate engagements over hours or minutes. Each echelon nevertheless needs a vision of the intended result and the conditions required to produce it. [AP] (Ch 4, “Shaping the Action,” pp. 83–84)

The Notes connect this discussion to the doctrinal ideas of an area of influence and an area of interest, borrowing their definitions from *Joint Publication 1-02*. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 105)

### Decisionmaking

Every action follows from a decision or nondecision. Failure to decide through lack of will surrenders initiative, while consciously postponing action for a reason is itself a decision. [AP] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” p. 84)

> “any decision is generally better than no decision.”

[V] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” p. 84)

Decisions must account for enemy reactions because each will acts upon and adapts to the other. Time is often the decisive factor: whoever repeatedly decides and implements faster gains a cumulative advantage. Timely action therefore limits consideration to essential factors, although deliberate situations without time pressure should not be rushed needlessly. [AR] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” pp. 84–85)

Military decisionmaking is not mathematical computation. It combines situational awareness of the problem’s essence with creative construction of a practical solution, drawing on experience, education, and intelligence. It may be intuitive in fluid situations and at lower levels or analytical when time permits comparison of alternatives. [AP] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” pp. 85–86)

Decisions should arise from awareness of unique circumstances rather than mechanical habit. Moral courage is required to decide under uncertainty and accept responsibility instead of waiting for complete information. No battlefield problem has a perfect solution; the task is to select a promising course with acceptable risk before the enemy does. [AR] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” pp. 85–86)

George Patton’s statement that a good plan executed violently now is better than a perfect one executed the following week is cited to support timeliness over unattainable perfection. [BT] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” p. 86; Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 105)

### Mission tactics

Mission tactics assigns a subordinate a mission without prescribing how to accomplish it. The subordinate receives freedom and a corresponding duty to take necessary action according to the situation, guided by an understanding of the higher purpose. [AP] (Ch 4, “Mission Tactics,” p. 87)

This frees senior commanders to concentrate on higher-level concerns. They prescribe methods only where coordination requires it and intervene in subordinate execution by exception. Subordinates adapt and report what they have done rather than waiting for permission. [AP] (Ch 4, “Mission Tactics,” p. 87)

Mission tactics forms a contract. The senior provides guidance, support, and freedom from unnecessary prescription; the subordinate acts responsibly and loyally within the senior’s intent and the proper limits of authority. [AR] (Ch 4, “Mission Tactics,” pp. 87–88)

Subordinates require topsight: an understanding of how their actions fit the larger situation. Unity results from harmonious initiative, lateral coordination, and higher guidance rather than imposed control over every action. [AP] (Ch 4, “Mission Tactics,” p. 88)

The Notes connect mission tactics to mission-type orders as defined in *Joint Publication 1-02*. They borrow topsight from David Gelernter as the overhead perspective revealing how parts form a whole. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” pp. 105–106)

### Commander’s intent

Commander’s intent supplies the context within which subordinates can depart from an obsolete plan while remaining aligned with higher aims. Every mission contains a task and a purpose: the task says what action is required, sometimes where and when; intent explains why. [AP] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” pp. 88–89)

> “Of the two, the intent is predominant.”

[V] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” p. 89)

Intent endures longer than a task because changing circumstances may invalidate the assigned action while leaving its purpose relevant. Intent flows downward: each commander derives a concept of operations and subordinate missions from the intent received above, creating continuity for bottom-up initiative. [AR] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” p. 89)

Intent can often be expressed concisely as a task followed by an in-order-to purpose. The source’s example is controlling a bridge to prevent enemy escape across a river. Amplification may sometimes be needed, but a complicated statement fails because subordinates cannot keep it constantly in mind. [AE] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” pp. 89–90)

Seniors carry the burden of explaining purpose clearly without inhibiting initiative; subordinates carry the burden of understanding. Subordinates should understand intent at least two command levels above their own. [AP] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” p. 90)

The Notes borrow the formal definition of mission as task together with purpose from *Joint Publication 1-02*. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 106)

### Main effort

The main effort is the unit responsible for the action currently most critical to success. It becomes the focal point for combat power and receives priority support; other units understand their actions in relation to supporting it. [AP] (Ch 4, “Main Effort,” pp. 90–91)

Designating a main effort commits the commander to a particular path to decision and makes other actions secondary. It should be directed where success will most affect the enemy and offers the best prospect of accomplishing the whole mission. This concentrates strength and necessarily accepts risk elsewhere. [AR] (Ch 4, “Main Effort,” p. 91)

The main effort should attack a center of gravity through a critical vulnerability. It can shift as the situation changes, redirecting resources toward the unit now most important. Such shifts should generally exploit success rather than reinforce failure. [AP] (Ch 4, “Main Effort,” pp. 91–92)

### Surfaces, gaps, and reconnaissance pull

Surfaces are enemy strengths and gaps are enemy weaknesses. Maneuver seeks to avoid the former and penetrate through the latter because matching friendly strength against weakness reduces losses and increases the prospect of decisive effects. Existing gaps should be exploited; if none exist, they should be created. [AP] (Ch 4, “Surfaces and Gaps,” p. 92)

Gaps and surfaces may exist in time, space, capability, or physical disposition. A boundary between units, a temporary exposure, a seam in air defense, or an unprepared infantry force can be a gap; a consolidated position or technological superiority can be a surface. [AP] (Ch 4, “Surfaces and Gaps,” p. 92)

Classification depends on the friendly force. A forest can be a surface for armour because it restricts vehicles but a gap for infantry able to infiltrate. Enemy deception can also make a surface appear to be a gap. [AE] (Ch 4, “Surfaces and Gaps,” pp. 92–93)

Because gaps are fleeting, aggressive reconnaissance must locate them and flexible forces must exploit them rapidly. If the designated main effort encounters strength while another unit finds a gap, the commander can shift the main effort and pull combat power through the opening instead of pushing it according to a rear-imposed scheme. [AE] (Ch 4, “Surfaces and Gaps,” p. 93)

The Notes identify these alternatives as reconnaissance pull and command push and cite William Lind’s *Maneuver Warfare Handbook*. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 106)

### Combined arms

Combined arms fully integrates different arms so that an enemy’s action to counter one creates vulnerability to another. Its object is a dilemma rather than a single solvable problem. [AP] (Ch 4, “Combined Arms,” pp. 93–94)

At fire-team level, automatic-weapon fire pins an enemy and makes him vulnerable to grenades; movement to escape the grenades exposes him to the automatic weapon. [AE] (Ch 4, “Combined Arms,” p. 94)

At MAGTF level, assault-support aircraft concentrate ground forces for a breakthrough; artillery and close air support assist the penetration; deep air support interdicts reinforcements; and each supporting arm engages targets for which it is best suited. [AE] (Ch 4, “Combined Arms,” pp. 94–95)

The enemy must expose himself to infantry to avoid supporting fires or expose himself to those fires to resist infantry. Reinforcements must move quickly to block penetration, but avoiding deep air attack forces them off roads and slows them. The integrated design makes every available enemy response harmful. [AE] (Ch 4, “Combined Arms,” pp. 94–95)

### Maneuver warfare as a state of mind

The concluding argument rejects a formulaic definition based on particular methods. Maneuver warfare resides in how Marines understand and act within conflict, from Marine expeditionary force commander to fire-team leader and across amphibious or sustained operations, high or low intensity, differing enemies, and differing terrain. [AR] (Ch 4, “Conclusion,” p. 95)

Its state of mind combines bold will, intellect, initiative, and ruthless opportunism. It seeks moral and physical dislocation by avoiding strength, exploiting vulnerabilities rapidly, and striking where the enemy will be hurt most. The publication’s final formulation is a philosophy for producing decisive effect at the least possible friendly cost—fighting intelligently rather than relying on brute expenditure. [AR] (Ch 4, “Conclusion,” pp. 95–96)

## Positions the publication explicitly frames against

- *Doctrine as a fixed body that can stagnate.* An adaptive doctrine must evolve with experience, theory, and war’s changing forms. [AP] (Foreword; Preface)
- *War as action against an inert object.* The enemy is an independent will that resists, adapts, and counteracts. [AR] (Ch 1, “War Defined,” pp. 3–4)
- *Certainty as a prerequisite for action.* Information remains incomplete and delay can surrender initiative. [AR] (Ch 1, “Uncertainty,” pp. 7–9; Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” pp. 84–86)
- *War as orderly clockwork.* Plans, communications, and control inevitably degrade under friction and reciprocal action. [AR] (Ch 1, “Disorder,” pp. 10–12)
- *Complete central control.* War’s distributed complexity and local knowledge make total centralisation inconsistent with its nature. [AR] (Ch 1, “Complexity,” pp. 12–13; Ch 4, “Philosophy of Command,” pp. 77–81)
- *Reduction of war to technology, equipment, or force ratios.* Such approaches omit human will and moral and mental forces. [AR] (Ch 1, “The Human Dimension,” pp. 13–14; “Physical, Moral, and Mental Forces,” pp. 15–17)
- *Romanticising or sanitising war.* Violence, bloodshed, destruction, suffering, danger, and fear are essential realities. [AR] (Ch 1, “Violence and Danger,” pp. 14–15)
- *Military force as a universal solution to political problems.* Military action must serve achievable policy and can create unintended political consequences. [AR] (Ch 2, “War As an Act of Policy,” pp. 23–25)
- *Treating small wars and operations other than war as merely lesser conventional wars.* They can demand qualitatively different preparation and methods. [AP] (Ch 2, “The Spectrum of Conflict,” pp. 26–28)
- *A rigid offense–defense dichotomy.* Each contains the other, and transitions are continuous and situational. [AR] (Ch 2, “Initiative and Response,” pp. 33–35)
- *Systematic destruction as the only route to victory.* Maneuver seeks systemic incapacitation through selected weakness and disruption. [AR] (Ch 2, “Styles of Warfare,” pp. 36–39)
- *A fixed formula for combat power.* Its components and their relative effects are unique to each situation. [AP] (Ch 2, “Combat Power,” pp. 39–40)
- *Direct attack into enemy strength.* Combat power should reach consequential strength through a critical vulnerability. [AR] (Ch 2, “Centers of Gravity and Critical Vulnerabilities,” pp. 45–47)
- *A zero-defects culture.* Punitive intolerance of honest mistakes suppresses the initiative maneuver warfare requires. [AR] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” pp. 57–58)
- *Yes-men and rank-protected decisionmaking.* Candour before a decision and loyal execution afterward are required. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professionalism,” p. 58)
- *Canned exercises as adequate preparation for war.* Without a free-playing opposing will, exercises remove war’s central dynamic. [AR] (Ch 3, “Training,” pp. 60–61)
- *Rote learning as the purpose of military education.* Schools should develop judgment and creative thought. [AP] (Ch 3, “Professional Military Education,” pp. 62–63)
- *Personnel as interchangeable by grade and speciality.* Assignment should account for ability and temperament. [AP] (Ch 3, “Personnel Management,” p. 64)
- *Technology as a cure for doctrinal or tactical weakness.* Technical advantage is temporary, support-intensive, and vulnerable to countermeasures and failure. [AR] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” pp. 65–67)
- *Information technology as justification for tighter control.* Precise positive control is incompatible with decentralised command. [AR] (Ch 3, “Equipping,” p. 67)
- *Maneuver as spatial movement only.* Advantage may also be temporal, psychological, or technological. [AP] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” p. 72)
- *Maneuver warfare as an aversion to firepower or physical destruction.* Attrition can be intense at the decisive point when it serves systemic disruption. [AR] (Ch 4, “Maneuver Warfare,” pp. 73–74)
- *Assuming the enemy thinks and values as friendly forces do.* Enemy orientation requires understanding the opponent on his own terms. [AP] (Ch 4, “Orienting on the Enemy,” pp. 76–77)
- *Detailed prescription of subordinate execution.* Mission tactics assigns purpose and responsibility while leaving methods to the subordinate except where coordination demands otherwise. [AR] (Ch 4, “Mission Tactics,” pp. 87–88)
- *Complex statements of intent.* Intent must be brief and compelling enough to guide decisions continuously. [AP] (Ch 4, “Commander’s Intent,” pp. 89–90)
- *Blind adherence to a predetermined main effort.* The main effort can shift to exploit a newly discovered gap or success. [AP] (Ch 4, “Main Effort,” pp. 90–92; “Surfaces and Gaps,” pp. 92–93)
- *Combined arms as simultaneous but independent employment.* Genuine integration forces every enemy counter to expose another vulnerability. [AR] (Ch 4, “Combined Arms,” pp. 93–95)
- *Maneuver warfare as a formula or fixed set of methods.* It is presented as a state of mind governing judgment and action. [AR] (Ch 4, “Conclusion,” pp. 95–96)

## Notes and doctrinal lineage within the source

- *Carl von Clausewitz, On War.* Supplies the opening account of friction; the duel or wrestler analogy; chance and nonlinearity; war’s political subordination; defense as a shield of blows; observations on boldness, numerical strength, surprise, and centers of gravity; and the warning against sanitising war’s violence. The Notes call it arguably the definitive treatment of war’s nature and theory and essential reading for Marine officers. [BT] (Notes, “The Nature of War,” pp. 97–98; “The Theory of War,” pp. 100–103; “Preparing for War,” p. 104)
- *Sun Tzu, The Art of War.* Provides epigraphs on defense and attack, avoiding strength, striking weakness, speed, unexpected routes, and enemy unpreparedness. The Notes describe the work as essential reading whose value persists despite its antiquity. [BT] (Ch 2 epigraph; Ch 4 epigraphs; Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 99; “The Conduct of War,” p. 104)
- *B. H. Liddell Hart, Strategy.* Supplies the Chapter 1 epigraph identifying human will as war’s chief incalculable. [BT] (Ch 1 epigraph; Notes, “The Nature of War,” p. 97)
- *A. A. Vandegrift, “Battle Doctrine for Front Line Leaders.”* Supplies the epigraph arguing that positions are usually lost because leaders decide they cannot be held rather than because they are physically destroyed. [BT] (Ch 1 epigraph; Notes, “The Nature of War,” p. 97)
- *Winston Churchill, The World Crisis.* Supports maneuver as a means of reducing slaughter through novel, rapid, and unexpected action and explicitly extends maneuver beyond the battlefield into time, diplomacy, mechanics, and psychology. [BT] (Ch 2 epigraph; Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 99–100)
- *Hans Delbrück, History of the Art of War Within the Framework of Political History.* Supplies lineage for strategies of annihilation or incapacitation and erosion. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 100)
- *Edward Luttwak, Strategy: The Logic of War and Peace.* Is recommended for the attrition–maneuver spectrum and further historical cases. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” p. 102)
- *John Boyd, “A Discourse on Winning and Losing.”* Supplies the observation–orientation–decision–action cycle used to explain tempo and the concept of implicit communication as a command instrument. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 102–103; “The Conduct of War,” p. 105)
- *Hans von Seeckt, Thoughts of a Soldier.* Supplies the Chapter 3 epigraph relating decision, preparation, execution, will, character, and intellect. [BT] (Ch 3 epigraph; Notes, “Preparing for War,” p. 103)
- *Earl H. Ellis, Advanced Base Operations in Micronesia.* Supplies the Chapter 3 epigraph insisting that Marines require environment-specific Marine training rather than generic occupational proficiency alone. [BT] (Ch 3 epigraph; Notes, “Preparing for War,” p. 103)
- *Sir William Slim, Defeat into Victory.* Supplies the Chapter 4 epigraph compressing the principle of war into striking quickly and forcefully where the enemy is most vulnerable and least prepared. [BT] (Ch 4 epigraph; Notes, “The Conduct of War,” pp. 104–105)
- *George S. Patton, Jr., War As I Knew It.* Supports rapid execution of a good plan over delayed pursuit of perfection. [BT] (Ch 4, “Decisionmaking,” p. 86; Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 105)
- *David Gelernter, Mirror Worlds.* Supplies topsight as the whole-system perspective showing how the parts fit together. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” pp. 105–106)
- *William Lind, Maneuver Warfare Handbook.* Supplies the reconnaissance-pull and command-push terminology. [BT] (Notes, “The Conduct of War,” p. 106)
- *Joint Publication 1-02.* Supplies formal definitions for the levels of war, national and military strategy, combat power, centers of gravity, force planning, doctrine, maneuver, areas of influence and interest, mission-type orders, and mission. [BT] (Notes, “The Theory of War,” pp. 100–103; “Preparing for War,” pp. 103–104; “The Conduct of War,” pp. 105–106)
